description:
Welcome to Polaris Nexus!

We are a Saudi-based team participating virtually in the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. Our team brings together expertise in Software Engineering, Artificial Intelligence, Data Science, and Astronomy.

Our primary interest is the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge, where we aim to develop an innovative web application that uses NASA's astronomical data to visualize the sky, compare observations over time, and explore changes in celestial objects.
summary: Polaris Nexus is a public, bilingual (Arabic/English) web tool that turns NASA's SPHEREx infrared sky survey into a time-lapse anyone can explore. Type a star name or RA/Dec and every SPHEREx exposure of that patch streams live to your browser, reprojected north-up so motion, not rotation, is what you see. As images arrive, validated algorithms measure the object's motion and a wavelength-corrected light curve using the exact SPHEREx wavelength at each pixel. A 16-year mode joins WISE and NEOWISE (2010–2024) to SPHEREx at the same 4.6 µm colour. On the challenge targets the tool agrees with Gaia and published values: Barnard's Star and Epsilon Indi B are detected as movers, WISE 0855 moves 8.18″/yr over 16 years (within 1% of the published 8.1″/yr), the variable stars are correctly found to be stationary, and R Draconis' 247-day pulsation is recovered. Gaia and WISE overlays, known asteroids, data-quality flags, shareable and embeddable links, and an AI astronomer that explains results in plain words make it a discovery tool for citizen scientists. It picks up new SPHEREx data releases automatically.
details:
Polaris Nexus answers the challenge directly: enter coordinates (or a name, in Arabic or English) and watch SPHEREx images of that patch of sky play like a movie, so anything that moves stands out. It is built for the public — a guided start, a plain-language "What are we looking at?" card, an Explorer mode for everyone and a Scientist mode with the full measurements.

How it works

1. Find — the backend asks NASA/IPAC IRSA which SPHEREx exposures cover the position. Releases are discovered automatically (it moved from the Quick Release to Data Release 1 during development with no code change), and the newest official release wins when an exposure appears twice.

2. Stream — only the needed pixels are read from NASA's cloud copy of SPHEREx and pushed to the browser over WebSocket the moment each exposure is ready.

3. Align — each exposure is reprojected north-up onto one grid; bad pixels are masked using the SPHEREx flags (saturated star cores are kept, not erased).

4. Measure — a PSF fit locates the source to a tenth of a pixel in every exposure; motion is fitted visit by visit with a calibrated systematic floor so a stationary star is never reported as a discovery. Light curves compare exposures at the same wavelength (±2.8%, one spectral channel) read from each file's wavelength table, and a Lomb–Scargle search finds periods.

5. Look back 16 years — WISE (2010) and NEOWISE (2014–2024) W2 images are co-added per visit and placed on the same grid as SPHEREx band 6 (same 4.6 µm colour); a tracker follows the source visit to visit without any catalogue.

6. Explain — Gaia DR3 and CatWISE sources are drawn at the date of each image, known asteroids are labelled (IMCCE SkyBoT), quality flags are explained in plain words, and "Ask Polaris" (Google Gemini) opens targets, switches views and explains the measured numbers in Arabic or English.

Results on the challenge targets (measured by the tool)

- Barnard's Star: moving, 12.9σ, agrees with Gaia DR3 within 0.4σ.

- Epsilon Indi B: moving, 11.1σ, agrees with Gaia DR3 within 0.5σ.

- WISE 0855: invisible below ~4 µm, so it is measured in band 6 only; over 16 years it moves 8.18″/yr (published 8.1″/yr), detected at 392σ.

- RW Aurigae and R Draconis: correctly judged stationary. R Draconis' pulsation period comes out at 247 days (published 245.6 days).

- Also tested on new fields: Proxima Centauri's motion measured at 3.87″/yr (published 3.85″/yr).

Challenge suggestions covered

Coordinates in the URL and an embeddable viewer; easy updates with new releases; creative use of the 102 bands (exact per-pixel wavelength, detector selection, co-adds, live spectrum); adding and subtracting images (deep stack, difference view, blink); selectable field of view; Gaia and WISE overlays; data-quality flags; Astropy throughout.

Benefits and impact

Anyone — students, amateur astronomers, the Arabic-speaking public — can see real NASA infrared data change over time and understand what it means, and help spot moving objects such as brown dwarfs and asteroids. Results are honest: saturated stars are labelled "inconclusive" rather than given a misleading number, and mistakes we caught (e.g. a stationary star first flagged as a 6σ mover) are documented on the site's Science page.

Tools and languages

Python (Django, Django Channels, Astropy, pyvo, reproject, NumPy, SciPy, photutils), TypeScript (React, Vite, Three.js, Tailwind), WebSockets, Uvicorn, Docker; deployed on Cranl. 14 automated tests and a load test (200 simultaneous visitors locally with no errors; 50 on the live site with no errors).

What makes it creative

Live measurement while data streams; a 16-year time machine across three NASA missions at the same colour; a catalogue-free tracker; an Arabic-first experience that also highlights the Arabic heritage of star names; and scientific honesty built into the interface.
